analysis.one_liner: Locks in FDA's narrow definition of a new drug, so minor tweaks can't win fresh exclusivity.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law the FDA's current practice of defining a drug's "active ingredient" as its "active moiety" — the core molecule that does the work — when deciding whether a drug qualifies as a new chemical entity. That narrower reading means a company cannot win a fresh 5-year market exclusivity period just by patenting a new salt or ester of a molecule the FDA has already approved. Under current practice, brand-name makers sometimes find their way around this; the bill would close that door permanently.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and generic drug makers. Codifying the narrower definition keeps new salts and esters of already-approved molecules from getting a fresh five-year exclusivity period, so generic competition can arrive sooner and prices stay lower.

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces every reference to "active ingredient (including any ester or salt of the active ingredient)" with "active moiety" across the sections of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that govern new chemical entity exclusivity, priority review for rare pediatric diseases, and related FDA programs [S3].

The Congressional Research Service states that the FDA's existing practice of using the active moiety in these situations "tends to exclude some drugs from market exclusivity" — meaning fewer monopoly windows for minor chemical variations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, who would lose the ability to claim a fresh five-year exclusivity period for new salts or esters of molecules already on the market, and would face earlier generic competition on those variants.

drawbacks.text: Some chemically modified versions of a drug are genuinely safer or easier for patients to take, and supporters of broader exclusivity argue a fresh exclusivity period rewards companies for making those improvements rather than just launching the original molecule [S3, S2].

Because the FDA already follows the active-moiety practice, the bill mainly locks in the status quo rather than changing anything today; its value is preventing a future administration from widening the definition, which limits its immediate effect on prices [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but modest: it affects only the slice of new drugs built by adding a salt or ester to an already-approved molecule, and FDA already applies this reading. The cost falls on brand-name drug makers in the form of foregone exclusivity. On balance this is a low-cost, pro-competition change, though it is a narrow technical fix rather than a broad drug-price measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel of New York introduced the bill on October 31, 2019, joined by Reps. Guthrie, Schrader, and Hudson [S3, S1].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce; the next day it went to the Subcommittee on Health [S5, S1].
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].
The bill had only three cosponsors (two Republicans, one Democrat), giving it a bipartisan but very small base of support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo: the active-moiety reading stayed an agency practice rather than statute, and no new restriction on exclusivity took effect. Patients saw no change either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Eliot Engel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify FDA's active-moiety practice for new chemical entity exclusivity.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over drug law
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never reported it out of the Health Subcommittee for a markup or floor vote.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill, which sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew two Republican and one Democratic cosponsors, with no recorded opposition from either party.

industries.note: The bill would bar a fresh five-year exclusivity period for salts or esters of molecules the FDA has already approved, closing a route by which minor modifications extend monopolies. Exclusivity on those variants means higher prices for patients; ending it means earlier generic competition.
With fewer drugs qualifying as new chemical entities, generics can reach the market sooner for modified versions of existing drugs, and lower prices follow.
